A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same InvestESG research. Their main text, equations, figures, implementation details, and appendices are readable, and retained content can be matched across relocation and renumbering.

before.justification: v1 reports original IPPO simulations and empirical Schelling diagrams, including climate-risk, wealth, investment, resilience, and company-count results.

after.justification: v3 reports original simulations, retaining the principal experiments and adding larger-agent settings and tests of initialization, investment lock-in, uncertain damage, and bankruptcy.

M1.justification: The default environment equations, IPPO learner, network architecture, and rewards remain unchanged. Appendix 11 introduces optional procedural extensions: five-year action lock-in, randomly varying climate damage, and bankruptcy after three consecutive years with margins below -10%. These extend the benchmark without replacing its core design.

E1.justification: v3 adds evaluated scenarios with restricted investment flexibility, uncertain damage across companies and events, and persistent-loss bankruptcy, including combined damage/bankruptcy conditions. These substantially broaden the environmental conditions and decision constraints tested within the retained corporate climate-investment task.

E2.justification: IPPO remains the learned baseline, and the existing cooperative/defecting policies, disclosure controls, ESG-preference comparisons, and no-greenwashing comparator are retained. New citations to BenchMARL and macro-action reinforcement learning do not represent newly evaluated comparison algorithms.

E3.justification: v3 adds 10-company/10-investor and 25-company/25-investor configurations, empirically informed initialization, climate-event and bankruptcy metrics, and final-100-episode summaries. Reported training horizons also change: v3 Figure 10 extends to approximately 140,000 episodes versus 30,000 in v1 Figure 4, although v3 Appendix 10.1 still states 30,000. The actual budgets are therefore not consistently documented.

E4.justification: Appendix 11 substantially expands robustness analysis by testing dependence on initialization, decision frequency, damage uncertainty, bankruptcy rules, and their interaction. Larger-agent experiments also test whether the principal patterns persist at greater scale. Earlier resilience and company-count analyses remain present; their relocation is not an addition.

E5.justification: Both versions specify three differently seeded trials, standard-error reporting, and fixed climate-event seeds across training episodes. v3's endpoint error bars retain this uncertainty-reporting practice. No increased independent-run count, confidence-interval method, or formal significance-testing procedure is reported.

E6.justification: Existing learning curves and investment matrices are replaced, and substantial new results appear in Figures 11–13. Whereas v1 Figure 4 emphasizes benefits only at ESG preference 10, v3 Figures 4 and 10 report graded mean improvements across 0.5, 1, and 10. New findings include increased greenwashing under uncertain damage. Differing reported training horizons preclude interpreting these revisions as same-budget performance gains.

T1.justification: The principal mathematical formulation, including Equations 1–11, is retained in v3 Appendix 9. Appendix 11.4 adds a formal alternative assumption: company damage parameters follow Gaussian distributions clipped to [0,1], varying across companies and events. No new theorem or proof is introduced.

C1.justification: The central benchmark contribution and claims about ESG-conscious investment, market bifurcation, and climate information remain. However, v1's introduction and conclusion describe high ecological validity, while v3 narrows the positioning to a first-principles model offering directional insights rather than representing full real-world complexity.

C2.justification: v3 adds substantive explanations linking uncertain damage to capital-relative mitigation, short-term greenwashing incentives, and bankruptcy avoidance. It also explains slower learning under investment lock-in and expands the justification for simplified, computationally accessible modeling. These establish additional mechanisms and applicability boundaries beyond v1's discussion.

D1.justification: v3 documents an initialization recipe using 50% of companies spending 0.5–1% of capital on mitigation, specifies the added lock-in and bankruptcy settings, and clarifies that the retained company-count analysis uses investors with zero ESG consciousness. Table 1's network and PPO settings, framework support, and existing repository disclosure remain substantially unchanged.

R1.justification: The new Problem Setting section substantially develops the relationship to sustainable-investing equilibria, dynamic economic modeling, greenwashing, and principal-agent problems. Additional discussion connects the fixed-seed design to DICE/RICE models and adds relevant MARL and empirical calibration literature. This extends the scientific positioning beyond bibliographic updates.

P1.justification: v3 adds a dedicated Problem Setting section, replaces the equation-heavy main environment description with an overview, and relocates the detailed formulation to Appendix 9. Results are reorganized into declarative findings, resilience moves into the main text, and the discussion and appendix organization are substantially revised.

P2.justification: Figure 4 changes from learning curves to endpoint bars, with revised curves in Figure 10. v3 adds climate-event panels, a greenwashing zoom, and extensive multipanel robustness figures. The hard-coded greenwashing example moves from Figure 6a to Figure 9, while resilience plots move into the main text. Axes, legends, captions, and page layout also change substantially.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens the previously narrow empirical foundation by testing initialization, investment flexibility, uncertain damage, bankruptcy, and larger populations. Appendix 11 reveals meaningful conditions under which incentives change, improving understanding of the benchmark's limits. The first-principles framing also better calibrates policy-facing claims than v1's ecological-validity language. Inconsistent training-horizon documentation remains a material reproducibility weakness, but the broader assumption testing and more restrained positioning provide a clear net improvement.
